sentence: Many decisions arise from the accumulation of noisy evidence until it reaches a threshold.
This process continues until the evidence reaches a specific bound or limit.
In perception, this mechanism explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed and accuracy.
The strength of the signal also influences how much confidence a person feels.
Models predict that an increase in noise should lead to faster decisions and reduced accuracy.
Paradoxically, this extra noise is also predicted to lead to higher confidence.
Researchers used a sensory manipulation that mimics unbiased noise in the visual cortex.
They verified this method using neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT and MST.
For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions.
These subjects also showed greater confidence while their accuracy was minimally impaired.
The magnitude of these effects was in agreement with model predictions.
The results support the framework of the bounded evidence accumulation model.
Noise accelerates the movement of the decision variable toward the termination bounds.
This acceleration explains why decisions happen more quickly when noise is high.
Human subjects issued higher confidence ratings on trials with high volatility displays.
This effect was most noticeable when the motion strength was weak.
The bacteria Shigella flexneri uses an enzyme called OspI to modify human proteins.
OspI converts a specific glutamine residue at position 100 in the host enzyme UBC13 into glutamate.
This chemical change stops the UBC13 and TRAF6 proteins from working together.
The modification prevents the NF-κB pathway from starting a normal inflammatory response.
The bacterial modification inhibits the binding between UBC13 and the TRAF6 RING domain.
This change disrupts both the stable and transient interactions needed for protein binding.
The modification creates a new intramolecular salt-bridge within the UBC13 protein.
This internal bridge competes with the intermolecular salt-bridge that normally connects the proteins.
Electrostatic repulsion between the new glutamate at position 100 and the TRAF6 surface destabilizes the complex.
The negatively charged surface of the RING domain pushes the modified UBC13 away.
This study shows how a post-translational modification can block protein-protein association.
The modification works by destabilizing transient complexes even away from the main interface.
Normally, the UBC13 and TRAF6 complex helps the body fight off infections.
The bacterial enzyme silences this immune signaling to help the pathogen survive.
The competition for salt-bridges prevents the two proteins from sticking together properly.
This specific electrical competition is a key part of the bacterial defense strategy.
Working memory depends on large-scale network interactions between different brain regions.
Working memory is the ability to hold and use information for short periods.
Brain regions exchange information through the synchronization of rhythmic neuronal activity.
These rhythmic waves occur when many brain cells send signals at the same time.
Researchers used transcranial alternating current stimulation to manipulate brain rhythm synchronization.
This tACS method uses low-level electrical currents at a 6 Hz frequency.
Induced synchronization improved working memory performance when cognitive demands were high.
This improvement was seen during a difficult 2-back memory task.
The impact of external manipulations depends on the participant's underlying cognitive state.
Researchers used fMRI scans simultaneously with tACS to track these changes.
Synchronous tACS increased parietal activity which correlated with faster response times.
The parietal region is a brain area involved in processing sensory information.
Altering phase synchrony through tACS can control long-range network interactions.
The timing of electrical pulses determines how well different brain areas communicate.
The study demonstrates a causal link between brain synchronization and demanding cognitive tasks.
This finding could help develop treatments for people with memory impairments.
Stimulation was applied specifically to the right frontoparietal network of the brain.
The right frontoparietal network is a group of regions that coordinate attention.
The granular retrosplenial cortex is essential for spatial navigation and other behaviors.
Damage to this brain region causes disorientation in familiar places.
Researchers used optogenetic circuit mapping in mice to study this region.
This method uses light to control and track specific brain circuits.
The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum activate low-rheobase pyramidal cells.
These unique cells process spatial information within the granular retrosplenial cortex.
The claustrum and anterior cingulate control neighboring regular-spiking cells instead.
These regular-spiking cells primarily handle non-spatial information from different sources.
Precise structural organization in layer 1 allows for this parallel processing.
The arrangement of axons and dendrites keeps these two pathways separate.
Low-rheobase neurons compute the speed of head rotation from direction inputs.
Synaptic dynamics of thalamic inputs allow for the robust encoding of speed.
Low-rheobase neurons are ideally positioned for spatial orientation computations.
These neurons comprehensively encode both speed and directional information.
These cells contribute to orientation computations in the superficial cortex.
This positioning helps the brain maintain a sense of direction during navigation.
The granular retrosplenial cortex is involved in learning, memory, and planning.
Excitable low-rheobase cells are unique among pyramidal cells in this region.
Stable flower shapes are important for the reproductive success of many plants.
These shapes must be robust to survive changes in the environment.
The plant Arabidopsis thaliana always produces flowers with exactly four petals.
This invariant petal number is a key feature of this species.
The related species Cardamine hirsuta has a variable number of petals.
Its flowers typically have between zero and four petals each.
Divergence in the gene APETALA1 explains why these two species differ.
This gene, also called AP1, regulates how flowers develop in plants.
The Arabidopsis version of AP1 ensures robustness by masking other genetic effects.
It hides the influence of quantitative trait loci that change petal count.
The Cardamine version of AP1 fails to complement this masking function.
Differences in regulatory regions of the gene cause this functional divergence.
Cardamine hirsuta maintains variable petal numbers despite having standing genetic variation.
The species could produce four-petalled flowers but keeps its variable form.
Masking occurs through epistatic interactions between the gene and other loci.
Arabidopsis AP1 hides the effects of at least nine different loci.
This divergence likely resides in regulatory regions rather than coding sequences.
These regions act as control switches for when the gene is active.
Physical trauma, disease, and aging can damage the human gastrointestinal tract.
These factors cause many health issues in the human digestive system.
Researchers used laser-capture microdissection and RNA-seq to study the planarian flatworm.
The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is a model for studying organ regeneration.
The study identified 1,844 transcripts that are enriched in the planarian intestine.
This method found hundreds of transcripts missed by previous single-cell profiling.
The planarian intestine transcriptome is similar to the human duodenum and liver.
These tissues share genes related to nutrient storage and innate immunity.
The flatworm gut also shows similarities to the human small intestine and gallbladder.
This conservation shows that digestive physiology is similar across different species.
Gene expression varies along the mediolateral axis of the planarian intestine.
Specific goblet cells are restricted to the medial regions of the gut.
The transcription factor gli-1 regulates the regeneration of these goblet cells.
Another factor called RREB2 regulates the maintenance of these same cells.
The researchers developed the website plangut.omrf.org to share their data.
This resource helps others study how the digestive system repairs itself.
Laser-capture microdissection allows scientists to isolate specific subregions from within a tissue.
Schmidtea mediterranea can regrow its entire gut after an injury.
Mitochondria are essential for cellular metabolism and must use quality control to remove misfolded proteins.
Damaged proteins can harm the cell if they are not properly cleared away.
Researchers studied this process in yeast using temperature-sensitive proteins that unravel when heated.
The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae serves as a model to observe these clean-up operations.
The ubiquitin-proteasome system degrades these proteins directly from the mitochondrial outer membrane.
This system acts like a molecular machine to break down the misshapen proteins.
The ubiquitin ligase enzymes Ubr1 and San1 are required to tag the proteins.
These ligases attach a molecular label that marks the damaged proteins for destruction.
Degradation also requires the SSA family of Hsp70 and the Hsp40 chaperone Sis1.
Chaperones are specialized proteins that help recognize and handle other misfolded proteins.
A mitochondrial pool of the protein Ubx2 helps the Cdc48 complex remove substrates.
Ubx2 acts as a necessary partner to help pull the proteins away.
This mitochondrial-associated degradation pathway is distinct from the ER-associated degradation pathway.
The unique combination of factors makes this specific pathway different from others.
The SSA1 chaperone is specifically required for the tagging of these proteins.
This finding confirms that specific chaperones assist in the removal process.
MicroRNAs are small molecules that help control how genes are used in cells.
One specific molecule called miR-9 is very common in the brain.
The role of miR-9 in dendritic and synaptic development was previously unknown.
Dendrites are tree-like branches on neurons that help cells connect to each other.
Researchers developed a transgenic miRNA sponge mouse line to conditionally inactivate miR-9.
This sponge technique uses a trap to soak up and disable the molecule.
The study found that miR-9 controls dendritic growth and synaptic transmission in vivo.
Synaptic transmission is the process of sending signals between different nerve cells.
This molecule promotes growth by causing the downregulation of a protein called REST.
REST is a transcriptional repressor that normally switches off certain genes.
When miR-9 was disabled, the neurons had shorter and less complex branches.
This confirms that the molecule is necessary for building healthy brain connections.
Reducing the REST protein allows genes needed for growth to stay active.
An increased REST level is the major cause of the growth problems.
These microRNAs are conserved noncoding RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription.
This means they act as a control system for protein production.
Disease spread by mosquitoes peaks at intermediate temperatures and falls at extremes.
Mosquito survival and performance depend on the temperature of their environment.
Researchers built a mechanistic model for the thermal response of Ross River virus.
This pathogen is found in Australia and the Pacific Islands and could emerge globally.
Transmission of the virus peaks at a moderate temperature of 26.4°C.
This specific temperature is the optimal point for the disease to spread.
The thermal limits for transmission are 17.0°C and 31.5°C.
The disease cannot spread effectively when it is too cold or too hot.
Transmission is year-round in the tropics but seasonal in temperate areas.
Low temperatures in southern regions prevent the virus from spreading all year.
Climate warming will likely increase transmission in temperate areas of Australia.
Warming may decrease transmission in tropical areas that are already very hot.
Using a nonlinear model is essential for predicting responses to climate change.
These models accurately predict how disease variation changes with the weather.
The virus infects thousands of people each year and causes joint pain.
Ross River virus is the most common mosquito-borne disease in Australia.
Temperature-based predictions match the actual patterns of human infections observed in Australia.
The motor cortex in the brain produces waves called beta oscillations.
The specific behavioral effects of these waves have remained unresolved for decades.
Researchers used electrode arrays to record brain activity in three male rhesus macaques.
The team monitored neural signals while the monkeys performed specific tasks.
The monkeys used neurofeedback to volitionally control their own beta oscillations.
After reaching a specific wave level, the monkeys performed an arm reach.
A reduction in beta power led to faster movement onset times.
An increase in these waves caused the monkeys to start moving slower.
Neural activity shifts farther from a movement onset state during beta oscillations.
The brain must travel a greater neural distance to trigger a movement.
These findings show that beta frequencies are a marker of slowed movement onset.
This explains why high beta activity delays the start of physical actions.
High beta power keeps the motor system away from the movement threshold.
This distance explains the delay seen before the monkeys began their reach.
The study confirms that beta power levels directly predict movement start times.
Lowering these oscillations allows the brain to initiate movement much more quickly.
Viruses like Marburg and Dengue benefit from the activation of a protein called Nrf2.
Nrf2 is a transcription regulator that typically helps human cells manage stress and antioxidants.
Sulforaphane is a natural product found in cruciferous vegetables that activates Nrf2.
Vegetables like broccoli produce Sulforaphane when they are chopped or chewed.
Sulforaphane blocks HIV infection in primary human macrophages but not in T cells.
Macrophages and T cells are both important types of immune cells in the body.
Reducing Nrf2 levels using siRNA boosted HIV infectivity in primary macrophages.
This reduction also diminished the effectiveness of Sulforaphane treatment against the virus.
Sulforaphane treatment blocks HIV infection after entry but before 2-LTR circles form.
The virus enters the cell but cannot finish preparing its genetic material.
The anti-viral effect of Nrf2 does not involve the proteins SAMHD1 or MX2.
These two proteins were not upregulated during the treatment process.
Activating cellular anti-viral defenses like Nrf2 may provide new therapeutic alternatives.
This discovery highlights a novel way to trigger inhibition of HIV infection.
The drug did not use common defense proteins to fight the virus.
This result was surprising because Nrf2 does not activate recognized anti-viral genes.
Arboviruses are viruses spread by insects that cause increasing illness and death worldwide.
These viruses include common diseases like dengue and Zika.
A study in the Dominican Republic compared a dengue epidemic and a Zika outbreak.
Researchers looked at how these two viruses affected the same local population.
About 75% of dengue cases occurred in people before the age of 20.
In contrast, only 42% of Zika cases occurred in that same young age group.
Reported Zika infections were highly clustered among females at 73.8% of cases.
This percentage shows that women reported the illness much more often than men.
Guillain-Barre syndrome rates were 0.62 in males and 0.57 in females per 10,000.
This syndrome is a serious nerve condition sometimes triggered by a Zika infection.
Existing population-level dengue immunity had little impact on Zika attack rates.
Having had dengue before did not seem to change the risk of Zika.
Higher Zika reports in women may be driven by increased health-seeking behavior.
Public awareness campaigns specifically targeted women of reproductive age during the outbreak.
Media campaigns and screening are recommended for women of reproductive age.
These tools help identify infections in the group most at risk for complications.
Anabaena filaments develop a pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts under nitrogen deprivation.
These specialized cells are separated by about ten photosynthetic vegetative cells.
The study used fluorescence to track the transcription factor HetR.
HetR acts as a master switch to trigger the change into a heterocyst.
HetR expression fluctuations in nearby cells are coupled across two to three cells.
This coupling sets the scale for cellular interactions along the filament.
Correlations arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Molecules move between cells to coordinate their internal gene activity.
Fluctuations under nitrogen-replete conditions build up to form the final pattern.
Subtle gene activity exists even before the cells face nitrogen starvation.
PatS, SepJ, and HetR auto-regulation determine the distribution of expression fluctuations.
These proteins control how signals spread between the neighboring cells.
The inhibitors PatS and HetN act at different stages of development.
The study also found differences between septal proteins SepJ and FraC/FraD.
Cell-cell communication controls stochasticity to ensure a precise developmental pattern.
Talking between cells helps overcome random noise in gene expression.
Anabaena is a multicellular cyanobacterium that grows in long chains.
Specific proteins act as inhibitors to stop neighboring cells from changing.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings through a process called dual-adaptation.
This process occurs when people receive feedback for different movements in an alternating pattern.
Participants performed a target-pointing task by tapping a graphics tablet to hit screen targets.
The researchers manipulated the visual feedback and required participants to tap within one second.
The study used morphing to create target shapes ranging from spiky to circular.
These different shapes served as cues to tell the person which movement was required.
A Bayesian learning model called a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters was developed to describe this learning.
This model explains how new sensory information is combined with prior experiences.
Participants apply the mapping for the trained shape most similar to the current one.
Successfully learning these associations requires the person to have conscious awareness of the cues.
The rate of learning tends to slow down as the number of training pairs increases.
This happens because multiple pairs cause interference during the learning process.
The Bayesian model provides a possible mechanism for learning multiple visuomotor mappings simultaneously.
This mathematical framework helps explain how the brain manages several different movement adjustments.
Many countries lack the baseline data needed to plan public health programs for neglected tropical diseases.
Without this data, health officials cannot easily launch or scale up treatment efforts.
Researchers developed the Integrated Threshold Mapping methodology to map four specific diseases at once.
This ITM method tracks lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol determines if a disease has reached the threshold for public health intervention.
The protocol focuses on the need for treatment rather than providing exact prevalence figures.
Researchers compared the ITM methodology to the standard WHO methodology in Mali and Senegal.
The team tested the new combined method against the old disease-specific mapping protocols.
The ITM methodology reached the same conclusions as WHO methods for trachoma, filariasis, and helminths.
The new method also resulted in more targeted intervention recommendations for schistosomiasis.
The ITM methodology demonstrated an overall cost saving compared to standard mapping methods.
The integrated approach took about half as much time to implement in the field.
The ITM tool could facilitate the implementation of much-needed programs in endemic countries.
This tool helps resource-poor countries start health programs more easily.
Organ aging is associated with a reduction in the number of stem cells occupying their specialized niche.
The niche is a specific environment that houses and supports these cells.
In Drosophila female germline stem cells, Notch signaling levels increase as the organism ages.
Drosophila is a type of fruit fly used to study biological processes.
Notch signaling regulates the adhesion of germline stem cells to the niche by controlling E-cadherin expression.
E-cadherin is a protein that helps cells stick to their surroundings.
The loss of germline stem cells from the niche is partially mediated by the gene Sex lethal.
This gene helps drive the increase of Notch signaling during the aging process.
Notch signaling is regulated in opposite directions in the niche versus the stem cells during aging.
Notch activation in the niche is reduced with age while it increases in the cells.
These findings regarding Notch signaling and cell adhesion may be relevant to metastatic cancer cells.
In these cancer cells, Notch signaling also suppresses how well cells stick together.
Sex lethal acts as an RNA-binding protein to control the Notch pathway.
The protein regulates how the Notch signal changes over time in the fly.
HIV infection currently cannot be cured but can be controlled using anti-retroviral drugs.
These drugs work by preventing the virus from making copies of itself.
Computational models help predict the most effective drug combination for an individual patient.
The best treatment depends on the specific genetic makeup of the virus.
Existing models rely on sequence data and ignore the chemical similarity of drugs.
Older tools did not consider how different drugs are related to each other.
Researchers applied proteochemometric models that combine chemical properties and protein target data.
This method looks at both the virus proteins and the drug structure.
The proteochemometric models outperformed sequence-only models in resistance classification.
The new models achieved a lower prediction error of 0.76 log units.
The study identified new resistance-conferring mutations like T216M in HIV Reverse Transcriptase.
Some of these genetic changes were previously unknown to the scientific community.
The models achieved an 84% prediction rate on the Stanford University HIV resistance database.
This result shows the model works well on real-world patient data.
The system includes an applicability domain to inform users about prediction reliability.
This feature helps doctors understand how much to trust each specific result.
Staphylococcus aureus uses a protein called ClfB to live inside the human nose.
This protein helps the bacteria stick to the lining of the nasal passage.
ClfB is also a major virulence determinant during skin and soft tissue infections.
These skin and soft tissue infections are often referred to as SSTIs.
The protein promotes abscess formation by binding to a host protein called loricrin.
Loricrin is found within the walls of the infected skin tissue.
Bacteria lacking ClfB cause smaller abscesses and a reduced bacterial burden in mice.
A reduced bacterial burden means fewer bacteria are present in the skin.
A vaccine using ClfB and CpG triggers protective antibodies and T cells.
These antibodies stop the bacteria from sticking to the loricrin in the skin.
ClfB is a strong candidate antigen for next-generation vaccines against skin infections.
Targeting this specific protein could help prevent future S. aureus skin diseases.
The lack of ClfB significantly weakened the bacteria's ability to survive in the skin.
This reduction in survival was observed by day 3 and day 6 of infection.
Dengue virus causes about 100 million symptomatic infections every year.
This virus is the most common infection spread by mosquitoes.
Infection ranges from mild dengue fever to life-threatening dengue hemorrhagic fever.
Dengue hemorrhagic fever is a severe form that causes internal bleeding.
The mechanisms that trigger the transition to severe disease are not understood.
This transition usually occurs during a critical phase of the infection.
Researchers used mass spectrometry to analyze the sera of adult patients.
This method allows scientists to measure small molecules in the blood.
The study identified 29 metabolites that differ between mild and severe cases.
These differences were found during the critical phase of the illness.
Bile acids were 5 fold higher in patients with severe dengue.
High bile acid levels correlate with markers of liver injury.
Uric acid levels were 1.5 fold lower in severe dengue patients.
Lower uric acid may decrease the capacity of the antioxidant defense.
Elevated chenodeoxyglycocholic acid persisted into the recovery phase for severe patients.
This finding suggests that the infection has lasting effects on the body.
The identified metabolic pathways may serve as therapeutic targets for management.
These targets could help doctors develop new ways to treat the disease.
Cells must tightly control the levels of substrate receptor subunits in Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases.
This control is necessary to maintain the full repertoire of these CRL machines.
Misregulation of F-box proteins in SCF ligases is linked to diseases like cancer.
F-box proteins act as specific receptors that select which targets to destroy.
F-box proteins are typically broken down by an intact SCF complex through autocatalytic ubiquitylation.
This proteasome-mediated degradation ensures that the cell does not have too many receptors.
Researchers found a new pathway in yeast that destroys the F-box protein Met30.
This specific pathway targets Met30 only when it is dissociated from its partner Skp1.
The new Met30 degradation pathway requires Cdc53/Cul1 but is independent of Skp1.
This finding was unexpected because Skp1 is usually a central part of this machinery.
This non-canonical pathway is essential for chromosome stability and defense against heavy metal stress.
The cell uses this mechanism to survive exposure to toxic metals like cadmium.
A sub-complex of Cdc53, Rbx1, and Cdc34 performs biological functions without Skp1.
This discovery shows that parts of the ligase can work as a smaller team.
